dialogs.title: संवाद — The last call
dialogs.intro: A year has gone by. Rahul calls Ani, and this conversation closes the book — with the sentences you'll need every time you say goodbye to someone you care about.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.literal: hello, Ani — ji? I — Rahul — speak — -ing(masc.) — am.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: I can't hear you clearly. Please speak a bit louder.
lines.literal: voice — clear — not — come — -ing(fem.). a-little — force — with — speak.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Yes. I called to ask you this — when are you leaving?

lines.id: Until then, take good care of yourself. See you again, Ani.

notes: **On the phone, Indians say "I am speaking", not "it's me".** *मैं राहुल **बोल रहा हूँ*** = "it's Rahul". And to ask: **कौन बोल रहा है?** (who's this?). ⚠️ Saying *मैं राहुल हूँ* on the phone sounds like introducing yourself to someone in the same room; it isn't wrong, just not the custom.

**अपना — the word that replaces "my / your" when it points back to the subject.** *अपना ख़्याल रखिए* = "take care of **yourself**" — not आपका, because the subject is "you". ⚠️ Compare: *मैं **अपनी** किताब पढ़ती हूँ* (I'm reading **my own** book) versus *मैं **उसकी** किताब पढ़ती हूँ* (I'm reading **his/her** book). When the owner is the subject, **अपना** is required — using मेरा there sounds wrong to native speakers.

**The -इएगा form for warm, unhurried requests.** You met it in Units 6 and 12. Here two appear at once: **रहिएगा** (do stay) and **रखिएगा** (do keep). ⚠️ This form sounds much softer than the ordinary -इए, and it's perfect for goodbyes, good wishes, and requests that don't need doing right away.

**पता ही नहीं चला — worth learning as a whole.** Literally "the knowing didn't even move", meaning "I didn't even notice". It's used for time that flew by, which is exactly what you need at the end of a long journey. Another version: *वक़्त कैसे बीत गया* (where did the time go).

**याद करना versus याद आना — two ways of missing someone.** *मैं आपको याद **करूँगी*** = I'll remember you (I do the remembering). *मुझे आपकी याद **आएगी*** = I'll miss you (the missing comes to me). The second sounds deeper. ⚠️ Many Indians also just use the English word *miss* — *मैं आपको मिस करूँगी* — and that's perfectly normal.

**Texting: almost all Indians type Hindi in Latin letters.** *Kaise ho?*, *Kal milte hain*, *Theek hai bhai*. This is called Romanized Hindi, and it has no standard spelling — people write it the way it sounds. ⚠️ Don't be discouraged after all your work on Devanagari: you'll still need it for signs, newspapers, books and song lyrics, and knowing it makes other people's Latin spellings much easier to read.

**Goodbyes have levels, and choosing the right one means something.** **फिर मिलेंगे** (see you again) for every day. **अच्छा, मैं चलती हूँ** (well, I'll be off) when leaving a place. **अपना ख़्याल रखिएगा** (take care) for a warm farewell. **अलविदा** for a long parting. And **ख़ुदा हाफ़िज़** from Unit 12 among Urdu speakers. ⚠️ Ending a conversation with just *bye* is normal in big cities, but adding one Hindi sentence after it always feels different.

sections.title: This far — and where to go next

blocks.text: Twenty units ago, rows of letters hanging from a single line may still have looked like a fence. Now you can introduce yourself, shop, order food, ask the way, talk about days gone by and days to come, tell a doctor how you feel, and turn down an invitation without offending anyone. That is real A1 level, and it's no small thing.

head: What you've mastered
Unit
rows: Sentences with है, greetings and levels of politeness
Verbs that agree with the subject's gender
The past, ने, and the future
Daily life: market, streets, home, guests

blocks.title: Three habits that make it all stick
items: **Say something in Hindi every day, even just one sentence.** A language you don't speak evaporates much faster than one you don't read.
**Watch one episode over and over, not five episodes once.** Repetition is what turns "understanding after thinking" into "just understanding".
**Find one conversation partner.** Thirty minutes of talking to a human beats three hours of reading alone, and there's no shortcut around that.

blocks.text: The summary pages at the back of this book — verb forms, nouns, numbers, pronouns — are designed to be opened again and again, not read once. Take photos of them and keep them on your phone.

And one last sentence to take with you. When you say your first Hindi sentence to an Indian you meet — at the market, on the train, at a tea stall — watch their face. Six hundred million people speak this language, and very few of them have ever met a foreigner who bothered to learn it. The reaction you get isn't politeness; it's delighted surprise, and it almost always turns into a long conversation, an invitation for tea, and sometimes an invitation to dinner. That's the real reward of these twenty units, and it's far bigger than any page can promise. **आपको बहुत बहुत शुभकामनाएँ — फिर मिलेंगे!**
